CHAPTER 1 OF 4 · THIGH AND AMPUTATION BLOCKS

Anatomy: the sciatic nerve and who supplies the thigh

The thigh is five nerves wide: femoral in front, obturator on the inside, lateral femoral cutaneous on the outside, and at the back two: the sciatic nerve for muscle and bone and the posterior femoral cutaneous nerve for the skin. Every thigh plan starts here.

RAPID FIRE

The sciatic nerve (L4–S3) is the biggest nerve in the body: two nerves (tibial and common peroneal) in one sheath.
It leaves the pelvis below piriformis, passes midway between the ischial tuberosity and the greater trochanter, then runs down the back of the thigh on adductor magnus.
It has no skin branches in the thigh. The back of the thigh is the posterior femoral cutaneous nerve (S1–S3), a separate sacral plexus branch that runs beside it in the buttock and parts company at the gluteal fold.
Hamstring branches leave its medial side high in the thigh: a popliteal block spares them, a subgluteal block does not.
The higher you block, the more you catch; the lower you block, the shallower and safer it is.

The posterior femoral cutaneous nerve

A purely sensory nerve from S1–S3. It is a branch of the sacral plexus, not of the sciatic nerve: it leaves the pelvis with the sciatic nerve below piriformis and runs down under gluteus maximus superficial to it, beside the inferior gluteal vessels. High in the buttock it lies medial to the sciatic nerve; at the gluteal crease its side varies and on ultrasound it is often slightly lateral. At the gluteal fold it gives inferior cluneal branches (the lower buttock) and a perineal branch, then runs under the fascia lata down the middle of the back of the thigh, piercing it in branches to the skin as far as the popliteal fossa and often the upper calf.

Why it matters: at the gluteal crease a thin fascia separates it from the sciatic nerve, so a subgluteal sciatic injection often misses it. Higher up (transgluteal, parasacral) one injection catches both. For an above-knee amputation its territory is the posterior flap.

CHAPTER 2 OF 4 · THIGH · SCIATIC NERVE

Subgluteal sciatic block

The sciatic nerve at the gluteal crease, in the plane under gluteus maximus between the ischial tuberosity and the femur. It numbs everything below the knee except the saphenous strip, plus the hamstrings and the back of the knee joint, so it works above a mid-thigh cut (with femoral, obturator and lateral femoral cutaneous blocks). Its blind spot is the skin of the back of the thigh: the posterior femoral cutaneous nerve lies beside it behind a fascia and is often missed.

USE IT FOR

Above-knee amputation
Below-knee amputation with a thigh cuff
Knee surgery: the back of the knee
Foot and ankle when the popliteal fossa is out of reach
Tibial fracture analgesia; catheters
POSITION
Lateral, block side up, hips and knees flexed (or prone)
PROBE
Curvilinear, transverse at the gluteal crease
NEEDLE
100 mm echogenic (150 mm if obese), in-plane, lateral to medial
DOSE
20 ml of 0.5% ropivacaine (100 mg), 5 ml aliquots; 15 ml when it is one of several blocks
COVERS
Below the knee except the saphenous strip; the hamstrings; the back of the knee joint (not its skin). Not reliably the back of the thigh.

The 20-second version. Curvilinear probe at the gluteal crease. Two bones: ischium medial, femur lateral. Under gluteus maximus, a flat bright oval: that is the sciatic nerve. In-plane from lateral, under it first, then over it. 20 ml. Add a posterior femoral cutaneous injection if the cut is in the thigh.

Position

Lateral (Sims), block side up, the upper hip and knee flexed so the gluteal crease opens; the lower leg straight. Prone is easiest for scanning if the patient can manage it. Expose the foot to see the twitch. For a patient who cannot turn (fracture, sick, external fixator), use the anterior approach supine, or lift the leg (hip and knee flexed, held by an assistant) for a supine subgluteal approach.

Equipment
Low-frequency curvilinear probe (a linear probe may do in a slim patient)
100 mm echogenic short-bevel needle; 150 mm for the obese, the anterior or the parasacral approach
Nerve stimulator (dual guidance helps at this depth): set about 0.5 mA
20 ml of 0.5% ropivacaine in a 20 ml syringe, extension line, an assistant to inject; injection pressure monitoring if available
Monitoring, IV access, lipid emulsion and the toxicity kit within reach
Landmarks and scanning

Feel the ischial tuberosity and the greater trochanter. The nerve runs down roughly midway between them, a little nearer the ischium. Put the probe transverse on the gluteal crease between the two.

Two bones, one oval: find the ischium (medial) and the femur (lateral) as bright lines with shadows; the nerve lies between them, under the bright fascia of gluteus maximus.
Can’t see it? Tilt the probe (the nerve is very anisotropic); ask the patient to move the foot (the nerve rocks); or start in the popliteal fossa, where it is easy, and trace it up.
Depth: several centimetres, more in the obese and deeper again at the transgluteal level. Start with the depth set deep, then set the focus at the nerve.
Colour Doppler: a small artery runs on the nerve (from the inferior gluteal artery).
Needle approach

In-plane, lateral to medial, entering 1–2 cm lateral to the probe. The path is steep: angle the probe slightly (heel-toe) to see the needle better. Feel the give through the fascia under gluteus maximus. Aim for the lateral corner of the nerve. Out-of-plane from caudal works too and suits a catheter.

Sonoanatomy

Labels for an OSCE: gluteus maximus, the subgluteal space (the plane under it), sciatic nerve, quadratus femoris (or adductor magnus just below), the ischial tuberosity and the hamstring origin medially, the femur laterally, and the posterior femoral cutaneous nerve as a small dot superficial to the sciatic nerve.

Fluid that surrounds the nerve in the subgluteal plane. In practice: inject under the nerve first (it floats up), then over it, so it is ringed. A single injection along its back surface works less often. The nerve should float, not swell.

Dose

20 ml of 0.5% ropivacaine (100 mg)

In 5 ml aliquots, aspirating between, half under the nerve and half over it. As one of several blocks (an amputation), 15 ml or a lower concentration keeps the total within the maximum: see the amputation planner. For analgesia only, 0.2% is enough. Allow 20–30 minutes: a big nerve takes time.

Covers: The leg below the knee, ankle and foot except the saphenous strip; the hamstrings; much of the back of the knee joint (the obturator nerve supplies the rest); part of the femur. The back of the thigh only sometimes.

MECHANISM

At the gluteal crease the sciatic nerve is still one trunk: the tibial division (medial) and the common peroneal division (lateral) in one sheath. It has no skin branches in the thigh, but it still carries the branches to the hamstrings (from its medial side, in the upper thigh), the posterior knee joint branches and everything below the knee. The posterior femoral cutaneous nerve runs beside it under gluteus maximus but is separated from it by a fascia at this level, so fluid around the sciatic nerve often does not reach it.

HOW DENSE, HOW RELIABLE

Dense surgical anaesthesia below the knee and complete motor block (no knee flexion, no ankle or toe movement) when the nerve is surrounded. Onset is slower than at the popliteal fossa: test at 20–30 minutes, in the tibial (sole), common peroneal (dorsum, first web space) and sural (lateral foot) territories, and the back of the thigh if the posterior femoral cutaneous nerve matters.

WHAT IT MISSES
The saphenous strip (medial leg and ankle): add a saphenous or adductor canal block, or a femoral block.
The front, lateral and medial thigh (femoral, lateral femoral cutaneous, obturator).
The back of the thigh in many patients: add a posterior femoral cutaneous injection, or use a transgluteal or parasacral approach.
The hip joint (it is below the hip branches).
Complications and how to avoid them
Falls and weakness: no knee flexion and a foot drop. The patient cannot stand on the leg; warn them, protect the heel, use a splint or boot as needed.
Nerve injury: the sciatic nerve is big, deep and hard to see well; intraneural injection was seen on video in about one in six subgluteal blocks in one series (without lasting harm, but no comfort). Low current, low pressure, no paraesthesia, stop if the nerve swells. The common peroneal division is the more vulnerable.
Masked injury or compartment syndrome: after hip surgery (sciatic nerve at risk from retractors and dislocation) and in leg trauma, agree with the surgeon before blocking, or block after the neurological check.
Vascular puncture: inferior gluteal vessels at the higher levels; femoral and profunda vessels on the anterior approach. Deep and non-compressible at the transgluteal, parasacral and anterior sites: matters in the anticoagulated.
Local anaesthetic toxicity when it is one of four or five blocks: count the milligrams.
Pressure injury of the numb heel and the back of the leg; long-lasting block after high concentrations.
Practical pearls
Two bones, one oval: ischium medial, femur lateral, nerve in between under gluteus maximus.
Lost the nerve? Trace it up from the popliteal fossa.
Anisotropic: tilt the probe until the oval lights up.
Under it first, then over it: the nerve should float, not swell.
Twitch the foot, not the buttock or the hamstrings.
Subgluteal: the posterior femoral cutaneous nerve lies beside the sciatic nerve but behind a fascia, so the back of the thigh may stay sensate.
Higher (transgluteal, parasacral) catches the back of the thigh; lower (popliteal) spares the hamstrings.
Supine and can’t turn? Anterior approach, 6–8 cm deep, medial to the femoral vessels.
A big nerve is slow: allow 20–30 minutes before you test.
Sciatic block for a knee replacement masks a peroneal palsy: discuss first.
Four levels compared: parasacral, transgluteal, subgluteal, anterior

The higher you block, the more neighbouring sacral plexus branches you catch. The posterior femoral cutaneous and inferior gluteal nerves leave the pelvis with the sciatic nerve (the superior gluteal nerve above piriformis) and part company with it in the buttock; none of them is a branch of the sciatic nerve. The lower you block, the easier and shallower it is, and the more you spare. The levels figure in the anatomy chapter shows the same thing on a drawing.

Parasacral: catches the sciatic, posterior femoral cutaneous and often the gluteal nerves; deepest.
Transgluteal: sciatic, and often the posterior femoral cutaneous; best for an above-knee amputation.
Subgluteal: sciatic and hamstrings; the back of the thigh not reliably.
Anterior: supine; sciatic only, the back of the thigh stays sensate.

Infragluteal and the landmark (Labat, anterior) techniques
Infragluteal: a few centimetres lower again, where the long head of biceps femoris crosses the nerve; often shallow enough for a linear probe. Same blind spot for the back of the thigh.
Landmark (classic posterior, Labat): lateral, upper leg flexed; a line from the posterior superior iliac spine to the greater trochanter, a perpendicular from its midpoint, and the needle where that meets the line from the greater trochanter to the sacral hiatus. Nerve stimulator to a foot twitch at low current. Know it for the exam; use ultrasound in practice.
Landmark anterior: supine; the needle enters where a perpendicular from the junction of the medial and middle thirds of the inguinal ligament line meets a parallel line through the greater trochanter, and is walked medially off the femur to the nerve. Deep, and the femoral vessels are close.
The posterior femoral cutaneous nerve block

The posterior femoral cutaneous nerve (S1–S3) leaves the pelvis below piriformis with the sciatic nerve and the inferior gluteal vessels, runs down under gluteus maximus superficial to the sciatic nerve (medial to it higher in the buttock; at the gluteal crease its side varies and it is often slightly lateral), and then under the fascia lata down the middle of the back of the thigh. It supplies the skin of the back of the thigh and the popliteal fossa, often the upper calf, the lower buttock (inferior cluneal branches) and part of the perineum. It is purely sensory.

When it matters: above-knee and through-knee amputation (the posterior flap), incisions or skin graft donor sites on the back of the thigh, and a calf or popliteal fossa incision. It matters less for a thigh tourniquet than for an incision: the deep nerves matter most under a cuff, but the skin of the back of the thigh under it is still this nerve.

Ultrasound, subgluteal: from the sciatic view, look just superficial to the sciatic nerve, under gluteus maximus, for a small oval beside a small artery; search the whole superficial surface, as its side varies. A thin fascia separates the two nerves and usually stops fluid crossing between them, so give it its own injection: 5–10 ml of 0.5% ropivacaine (25–50 mg), counted in the total.
Higher up, one needle: at the transgluteal and parasacral levels it lies closer to the sciatic nerve, so the main injection often catches it.
Landmark, at the gluteal crease: a subcutaneous wheal along the crease, plus a few millilitres deep to the fascia at its midpoint (fanned), to catch the nerve before it pierces the fascia. In the mid-thigh, a subcutaneous line about 5 cm above and parallel to the popliteal crease catches its lower branches (with a popliteal block, for varicose vein surgery behind the knee).
Nerve stimulator: which twitch counts
Accept: a twitch of the calf or foot (plantar flexion, inversion, dorsiflexion or eversion) at about 0.3–0.5 mA. Inversion (tibial and deep peroneal together) suggests the tip is near the centre of the nerve and predicts the most complete block; eversion alone suggests you are on the peroneal side.
Don’t accept: a gluteus maximus twitch (you are still in the muscle, or on the inferior gluteal nerve) or a hamstring twitch alone (direct muscle stimulation, or a branch that has already left the trunk).
With ultrasound, use the stimulator as a safety monitor: a twitch at very low current (below about 0.2 mA) suggests the tip is touching or inside the nerve. No twitch does not prove you are outside it.
Catheters
How to place one, and the surgeon’s catheter

A subgluteal catheter gives days of analgesia for an amputation stump or a major foot and ankle reconstruction. Out-of-plane from caudal (the catheter then follows the nerve down), or in-plane from lateral; hydrodissect under the nerve with 5 ml, thread 3–5 cm past the tip, and inject through it while scanning. Tunnel and fix it well: the buttock is a hard place to keep a catheter.

In amputations the surgeon can place a catheter into the sciatic nerve sheath under direct vision before dividing the nerve: simple, reliable, no extra needle. The evidence for both is in the amputation chapter. Run dilute solutions (for example 0.2% ropivacaine); the leg is already weak or gone, so motor block matters less than toxicity.

Consultant corner
Seven subspecialty points
Two nerves in one sheath. The tibial and common peroneal divisions share a sheath down to the popliteal fossa in most people, but in about one in ten they are separate from the pelvis (the common peroneal division may even pass through or above piriformis). If you see two nerves high up, block both.
The obese patient. Injecting into the subgluteal space (the plane under gluteus maximus, on quadratus femoris) rather than chasing the nerve was about twice as fast in overweight patients, with the same success. Fascial-plane thinking works here.
The anticoagulated or septic patient. The transgluteal, parasacral and anterior sites are deep and non-compressible; the subgluteal is intermediate, the popliteal superficial. Use the lowest level that does the job, ultrasound and colour Doppler, a fine needle, and follow your anticoagulation guidance for deep blocks.
The hip. The back of the hip capsule is supplied by the nerve to quadratus femoris, sciatic branches and the superior gluteal nerve, which a parasacral block reaches and a subgluteal block does not. Parasacral plus a lumbar plexus block was the classic complete hip block; today PENG and fascia iliaca cover the front (see the hip page).
Knee surgery. A sciatic block for knee replacement gives good posterior analgesia but a foot drop that masks surgical peroneal nerve injury; PROSPECT does not recommend it. iPACK and a selective tibial block are the motor-sparing answers.
Dual guidance at depth. When the needle is hard to see (steep, deep, obese), the stimulator tells you which side of the nerve you are on, and injection pressure monitoring adds protection.
Fascial plane or perineural? At the subgluteal level both work; perineural (circumferential) spread gives faster, more complete block, the plane approach is quicker and arguably safer. Choose by the image and the patient.
Frontier: what’s new
Five things that are new or being tested
Naming. The 2024 ASRA–ESRA consensus names limb blocks by the nerve and the level: “sciatic nerve block, subgluteal” rather than a list of eponyms, so that trials and records compare like with like.
Percutaneous peripheral nerve stimulation. Fine leads placed near the sciatic and femoral nerves and stimulated for 60 days reduced chronic post-amputation pain in a small placebo-controlled trial, and the benefit lasted to 12 months in most of those treated. The leads do not numb or weaken, which makes them attractive for the stump.
Cryoneurolysis of the sciatic and femoral nerves did not reduce established phantom limb pain in a multicentre sham-controlled trial, and a 2026 pilot that froze all four thigh nerves in people with an above-knee amputation found no benefit either; the large sciatic nerve may simply be too big to freeze through.
Surgery for the nerve itself. Targeted muscle reinnervation joins the cut nerve ends to motor branches of nearby muscles. In a small randomised trial in amputees with established neuroma or phantom pain, it was favoured over excising the neuroma and burying the nerve in muscle; it is increasingly done at the primary amputation. Ask your surgeons whether they do it: it changes where the catheter can go.
Perineural catheters at home. A six-day ambulatory perineural infusion of ropivacaine (sciatic and femoral, or brachial plexus) reduced established phantom limb pain a month later in a multicentre placebo-controlled trial, with little benefit left at a year (see the amputation chapter).
Exam corner

PRACTICE QUESTION

Outline the anatomy of the sciatic nerve from the pelvis to the knee, as relevant to blocking it.

Model answer points
Roots L4–S3, from the sacral plexus; the largest nerve in the body; two divisions in one sheath: tibial (medial, L4–S3) and common peroneal (lateral, L4–S2).
Leaves the pelvis through the greater sciatic foramen below piriformis, with the posterior femoral cutaneous nerve, the inferior gluteal nerve and vessels, and the pudendal nerve (medially).
In the buttock: deep to gluteus maximus, on the posterior surface of the ischium, then on the gemelli, obturator internus and quadratus femoris, about midway between the ischial tuberosity and the greater trochanter.
In the thigh: on adductor magnus, crossed superficially by the long head of biceps femoris; branches to the hamstrings and the hamstring part of adductor magnus (short head of biceps from the peroneal division).
Divides near the apex of the popliteal fossa (level varies; high division in about one in ten).
No cutaneous branches in the thigh: the back of the thigh is the posterior femoral cutaneous nerve. Below the knee: everything except the saphenous territory.

PRACTICE QUESTION

Demonstrate the sciatic nerve at the subgluteal level on this volunteer. What is the subgluteal space? What will a block here not cover?

Model answer points
Lateral (or prone), hips and knees flexed; curvilinear probe transverse at the gluteal crease between the ischial tuberosity and the greater trochanter.
Identify gluteus maximus, its deep fascia, the ischial tuberosity (medial) and femur (lateral) with their shadows, quadratus femoris or adductor magnus deep, and the sciatic nerve: a flat hyperechoic oval or triangle between them.
Subgluteal space: the fascial plane between gluteus maximus (superficial) and quadratus femoris (deep), bounded by the ischial tuberosity and greater trochanter; the sciatic nerve runs in it.
Tricks: tilt for anisotropy; foot movement; trace up from the popliteal fossa.
Not covered: saphenous territory, anterior, lateral and medial thigh (femoral, LFCN, obturator), the hip joint, and often the back of the thigh (posterior femoral cutaneous nerve).

PRACTICE QUESTION

You have done femoral, obturator, lateral femoral cutaneous and subgluteal sciatic blocks for an above-knee amputation. The surgeon’s posterior skin incision hurts. Why, and what will you do?

Model answer points
The posterior thigh skin is the posterior femoral cutaneous nerve, which often escapes a subgluteal sciatic injection (separated by a fascia).
Options: an ultrasound-guided posterior femoral cutaneous injection superficial to the sciatic nerve (if the patient can be positioned), local infiltration by the surgeon along the posterior flap, or sedation and analgesia.
Count the dose already given before adding any more local anaesthetic.
Next time: block it deliberately, or choose a transgluteal level, which more often catches both.

PRACTICE QUESTION

During a nerve stimulator-guided sciatic block in the buttock you see a strong twitch of the buttock at 1 mA. Then a hamstring twitch. Interpret these, and give the endpoint you want.

Model answer points
Buttock twitch: direct gluteus maximus stimulation or the inferior gluteal nerve: too superficial, advance.
Hamstring twitch alone: direct muscle or a hamstring branch: unreliable, redirect.
Wanted: calf or foot twitch (inversion best, then plantar flexion; eversion or dorsiflexion means the peroneal side) at about 0.3–0.5 mA, lost below about 0.2 mA.
With ultrasound: the image and the spread are the endpoint; the stimulator is a safety monitor.

PRACTICE QUESTION

Describe the landmarks for the classic posterior (Labat) and the anterior sciatic nerve blocks. Why has ultrasound largely replaced them?

Model answer points
Classic posterior (Labat): lateral (Sims) position, upper hip and knee flexed. A line from the posterior superior iliac spine to the greater trochanter; a perpendicular from its midpoint, caudally; the needle enters where it meets the line from the greater trochanter to the sacral hiatus. Needle perpendicular to the skin; nerve stimulator to a calf or foot twitch.
Anterior: supine. The inguinal ligament line from the anterior superior iliac spine to the pubic tubercle is trisected; a perpendicular from the junction of its medial and middle thirds meets a parallel line through the greater trochanter. The needle passes posteriorly, is walked medially off the femur (lesser trochanter) and advanced to a foot twitch.
Both are deep, blind and rely on surface landmarks that shift with obesity and position; the anterior path passes close to the femoral vessels.
Ultrasound shows the nerve, the vessels and the spread; it allows a lower volume, fewer passes and a fascial-plane injection (the subgluteal space) when the nerve is hard to see. The landmark methods remain useful as a backup and in exams.

PRACTICE QUESTION

What would you tell a patient when consenting for a subgluteal sciatic block for foot surgery? What are the specific risks?

Model answer points
Expect a numb, heavy leg below the knee with a foot drop and no knee flexion for many hours (often into the next day with long-acting drugs).
Falls: do not walk on the leg until it has recovered; crutches or a splint or boot as advised; protect the numb heel and the back of the leg from pressure.
Nerve injury: transient tingling or numbness is fairly common; lasting injury is rare. Report weakness or numbness that has not recovered when expected.
Masking: the block can hide a surgical peroneal nerve injury or a compartment syndrome; agree with the surgeon beforehand when either is a risk (tibial fractures, knee surgery).
Also: block failure (backup plan), bleeding or bruising (deep site), local anaesthetic toxicity (rare), infection.

Amputation planner: above and below the knee under nerve blocks

The patient is often the sickest on the list: septic, on dual antiplatelets or anticoagulants, with a poor heart. Nerve blocks keep the blood pressure where it is and avoid the airway and the spine. The price is more needles, more milligrams and a plan for every nerve.

RAPID FIRE

Below the knee: two nerves. Popliteal sciatic + saphenous (adductor canal) or femoral.
Above the knee: five nerves. Sciatic, posterior femoral cutaneous, femoral, lateral femoral cutaneous, obturator.
Skip the obturator and the LFCN and the patient will need much more sedation: the medial and lateral thigh will hurt.
Count the milligrams before the first needle. Trim the strength, not the nerves.
A thigh tourniquet under blocks alone is a big ask: avoid it if you can.
Ask the surgeon to place a catheter in the sciatic nerve sheath before dividing it.
Who, and why blocks
The patient: diabetic, vasculopathic, often septic from wet gangrene; ischaemic heart disease and heart failure; renal impairment; on antiplatelets or anticoagulants after failed revascularisation; high opioid use for ischaemic rest pain. Surgery is source control: it rarely waits.
Spinal is excellent when allowed, but sepsis, dual antiplatelets or anticoagulation often rule it out. General anaesthesia in a septic patient with a poor heart risks haemodynamic collapse.
Peripheral nerve blocks keep the circulation stable, are compatible with most anticoagulation at superficial sites, and give hours of analgesia afterwards. In a Singapore series of ASA IV patients having above-knee amputation under blocks, about nine in ten needed no conversion to general or spinal anaesthesia; nearly all had some sedation, and those given only femoral and sciatic blocks needed more of it than those who also had the obturator (and LFCN) blocked.
Arterial line if septic or haemodynamically unstable; group and save or crossmatch, as blood loss depends on the level and on whether a tourniquet is used.

Close to the ceiling. Leave nothing for surgical infiltration; consider a lower strength.

Five nerves cross a mid-thigh cut. The suggested set trims the doses so that four blocks fit under the ceiling for most adults: transgluteal sciatic (which often catches the posterior femoral cutaneous nerve) at 15 ml of 0.5% (a smaller volume keeps the block dense), femoral (15 ml of 0.4%) and LFCN (5 ml of 0.2%) at their standard doses, and obturator at 0.375% (slower and less dense than 0.5%). A teaching set: agree your own with a consultant. Plan sedation as well: almost every patient in published series had some.

Sciatic, transgluteal: Often catches the posterior femoral cutaneous nerve as well (more often than subgluteal).
Choose an operation: the suggested set loads; then switch blocks on and off and change the doses. The leg shows what is numb (solid = dense, dotted = patchy) and where the surgeon cuts. The ceiling used here is 3 mg/kg of ropivacaine, a commonly used figure: use lean weight, and aim lower in the frail, in heart failure and in liver disease. Toxicity from several blocks adds up. A teaching tool, not a prescription.
Doing it: an above-knee amputation under blocks
Plan the dose first. Weigh the patient (lean weight), choose the set, write down the milligrams for each block. Have lipid emulsion in the room.
Sciatic first if the patient can be turned: it is the slowest. Transgluteal (more often catches the posterior femoral cutaneous nerve) or subgluteal plus its own posterior femoral cutaneous injection. Can’t turn? The anterior approach supine, or lift the leg (hip and knee flexed) for a subgluteal view from below.
Then supine, one position: femoral, lateral femoral cutaneous, obturator (proximal, or both divisions distally). A supra-inguinal fascia iliaca covers femoral and LFCN together but does not reliably reach the obturator.
Test each territory at 20–30 minutes: front, outer, inner and back of the thigh at the level of the cut; foot movement for the sciatic.
Sedation plan: titrated, airway-safe, with oxygen and capnography. Ketamine in small doses suits the opioid-tolerant. The surgeon can infiltrate a patchy area, within the dose.
Before the sciatic nerve is divided, ask for a perineural catheter in its sheath (or place your own) for the days after.

WARNING

Gaps that will show

Back of the thigh (posterior flap): posterior femoral cutaneous nerve missed by a subgluteal or anterior sciatic block.
Inner thigh and adductors: obturator. Femoral and fascia iliaca blocks do not reliably reach it.
Outer thigh: lateral femoral cutaneous.
The femur: supplied by all three big nerves; sawing hurts unless femoral, sciatic and obturator are all blocked.
Below-knee amputation
Popliteal sciatic + saphenous covers the skin, muscles, tibia and fibula below the knee. The saphenous block can be at the adductor canal; a femoral block does the same and also numbs the anterior thigh.
Block the popliteal sciatic nerve at or above the division so the lateral sural cutaneous branch (outer upper calf, the lateral end of the incision) is included.
A long posterior flap can reach the territory of the posterior femoral cutaneous nerve high on the calf in some people: if the top of the flap is sensate, the surgeon infiltrates or you add a posterior femoral cutaneous injection.
Anticoagulated patient: the popliteal fossa and adductor canal are superficial and compressible, which is why this is often the anaesthetic of choice when spinal is not allowed.
Guillotine (staged) amputation for sepsis, then a formal amputation days later: a catheter placed at the first operation can serve both.
Tourniquets

Vascular surgeons often amputate without a tourniquet; orthopaedic and trauma surgeons often use one. Tourniquet pain is a deep, ischaemic pain that builds with time; it needs all the nerves of the limb blocked above the cuff (sciatic, femoral, obturator, and the skin under the cuff) and even then is tolerated only for a limited period. For a below-knee amputation under a popliteal block, a calf or no tourniquet fits the block; a thigh cuff does not. The tourniquet guide on the foot and ankle page has more.

Catheters and phantom limb pain

Three kinds of pain follow an amputation: wound (residual limb) pain, which settles with healing; phantom sensations, which nearly everyone has; and phantom limb pain, pain felt in the missing part. About six in ten amputees report phantom pain at some point. Risk factors: severe pain before the amputation, a more proximal (above-knee) amputation, persistent stump pain, a lower-limb amputation and early phantom sensations. Mechanisms run from the cut nerve (neuroma, ectopic firing) through spinal sensitisation to cortical reorganisation.

Perineural catheters (most often placed by the surgeon in the sciatic or tibial nerve sheath, infusing for several days): pooled studies show lower pain scores after surgery; the opioid-sparing effect disappears when only randomised trials are counted; there is no demonstrated effect on phantom pain, chronic stump pain or mortality. Low risk, cheap, and patients are comfortable: worth doing, but don’t promise to prevent phantom pain.
A double-blind trial of perineural levobupivacaine 0.125% (a 10 ml bolus, then 8 ml an hour for four days) after above- and below-knee amputation found no difference in phantom pain at six months, but was underpowered; high early morphine use went with worse phantom pain later. A large UK multicentre trial of surgeon-placed catheters (several hundred patients) has been recruiting; results are awaited.
Pre-emptive epidural analgesia started the day before and continued after amputation did not prevent phantom or stump pain in a randomised trial.
Treating established phantom pain: a six-day ambulatory perineural infusion of ropivacaine (sciatic and femoral, or brachial plexus) reduced established phantom pain a month later in a multicentre placebo-controlled trial, with little benefit left at a year.
For the ward: regular paracetamol, an NSAID only if the kidneys allow, opioid by need (not by habit), and early pain team input. Gabapentinoids have not been shown to prevent phantom pain. Address pain before the operation: it is the strongest risk factor you can still change.
How a surgeon-placed sciatic catheter is usually set up

Before the sciatic nerve is divided, the surgeon passes a catheter (an epidural catheter works) into the nerve sheath, proximally for several centimetres, and brings it out through the skin away from the wound. A bolus (for example 10 ml of 0.125–0.25% bupivacaine-family local anaesthetic) is given before the end of the operation, then an infusion of a few millilitres an hour of a dilute solution for three to five days. Count it in the daily dose, label it clearly as a perineural line, and agree who removes it.

Consultant corner
Five subspecialty points
Mix to save milligrams? Many series used a long-acting drug mixed with lidocaine or mepivacaine for a faster onset and less long-acting drug. The toxicities add: count each drug as a fraction of its own maximum and keep the sum below one. Mixing shortens the block.
Lumbar plexus instead of three blocks? A lumbar plexus (psoas compartment) block covers the femoral and LFCN, and usually the obturator, in one injection, and with a parasacral or transgluteal sciatic it is the textbook anaesthetic for an above-knee amputation. It is deep, close to the epidural space and the kidney, and non-compressible: a poor choice in the anticoagulated, which is most of these patients.
Bilateral amputations: block and operate on one side at a time, and do the second side’s blocks only when the dose allows; or use a different anaesthetic for the second side.
Oedema and infection make the image poor and spread unpredictable: use the stimulator as well, scan away from infected tissue, and prefer levels above the infection.
Delirium, mortality and goals of care: thirty-day mortality after major amputation is high (in the Singapore series, about one in eight at 30 days and nearly half at a year). Blocks avoid opioid-heavy recovery, which helps with delirium; agree ceilings of care before the day.
Frontier: what’s new
Four things that are new or being tested
Targeted muscle reinnervation: surgeons join the cut nerve end to a motor branch of a nearby muscle instead of letting it form a neuroma. In a small randomised trial in amputees with established neuroma or phantom pain, it was favoured over excising and burying the nerve; it is increasingly done at the primary amputation. Regenerative peripheral nerve interfaces (the nerve end wrapped in a small free muscle graft) are an alternative nerve-end operation; they were not part of that trial.
Percutaneous peripheral nerve stimulation of the sciatic and femoral nerves for 60 days reduced chronic post-amputation pain in a small placebo-controlled trial, with benefit at 12 months in most of those treated.
Cryoneurolysis of the sciatic and femoral nerves did not reduce established phantom pain in a multicentre sham-controlled trial; a 2026 pilot freezing all four thigh nerves in above-knee amputees also found no benefit.
Ambulatory catheters: the six-day infusion trial suggests a window to treat established phantom pain at home; whether an early, longer perineural infusion can prevent it is the question the current catheter trials are answering.
Exam corner

MMED OSCE 2020

Which nerves need to be blocked for an above-knee amputation?

Model answer points
Sciatic nerve (above the cut: subgluteal, transgluteal, parasacral or anterior), for the hamstrings, the back of the femur and everything below.
Posterior femoral cutaneous nerve, for the skin of the back of the thigh (posterior flap): caught at the transgluteal or parasacral level, or blocked separately.
Femoral nerve, for the front of the thigh, quadriceps and much of the femur.
Lateral femoral cutaneous nerve, for the outer thigh.
Obturator nerve, for the adductors, part of the femur and a variable patch of inner thigh skin.

PRACTICE QUESTION

A 74-year-old with wet gangrene of the foot, on aspirin and clopidogrel, with an ejection fraction of 25%, is listed for a below-knee amputation tonight. Outline your anaesthetic plan.

Model answer points
Assess: sepsis severity, fluid status, heart failure, renal function, glucose, potassium, coagulation and the antiplatelet timing; goals of care.
Neuraxial is generally avoided on dual antiplatelet therapy; general anaesthesia risks haemodynamic instability.
Plan: ultrasound-guided popliteal sciatic + saphenous (adductor canal) or femoral block, superficial and compressible, with light sedation; arterial line if septic.
Dose: count the total (for example popliteal 15 ml 0.4% + adductor canal 10 ml 0.4% ropivacaine = 100 mg); lipid emulsion available.
No thigh tourniquet (or a calf one); ask the surgeon for a sciatic sheath catheter.
Postoperative: HDU if needed, multimodal analgesia, pain team, delirium prevention; discuss phantom pain.

PRACTICE QUESTION

What is phantom limb pain? How common is it, who gets it, and does a perineural catheter prevent it?

Model answer points
Pain felt in the amputated part, distinct from residual limb (stump) pain and from non-painful phantom sensations.
About six in ten amputees report it at some point.
Risk factors: severe pre-amputation pain, proximal (above-knee) level, persistent stump pain, lower-limb amputation, early phantom sensations.
Mechanisms: peripheral (neuroma, ectopic firing), spinal (central sensitisation), supraspinal (cortical reorganisation).
Perineural catheters lower early pain scores; no proven effect on phantom pain or chronic stump pain. Pre-emptive epidural did not prevent it in a randomised trial.
Treatment of established pain: multimodal and neuropathic agents, mirror therapy and rehabilitation; a six-day perineural infusion reduced established phantom pain at four weeks in one trial; targeted muscle reinnervation for neuroma-related pain.

STEP 1 OF 4 · SCAN

CHAPTER 1 OF 4 · THIGH AND AMPUTATION BLOCKS

Anatomy: the sciatic nerve and who supplies the thigh

The thigh is five nerves wide: femoral in front, obturator on the inside, lateral femoral cutaneous on the outside, and at the back two: the sciatic nerve for muscle and bone and the posterior femoral cutaneous nerve for the skin. Every thigh plan starts here.

RAPID FIRE

The sciatic nerve (L4–S3) is the biggest nerve in the body: two nerves (tibial and common peroneal) in one sheath.
It leaves the pelvis below piriformis, passes midway between the ischial tuberosity and the greater trochanter, then runs down the back of the thigh on adductor magnus.
It has no skin branches in the thigh. The back of the thigh is the posterior femoral cutaneous nerve (S1–S3), a separate sacral plexus branch that runs beside it in the buttock and parts company at the gluteal fold.
Hamstring branches leave its medial side high in the thigh: a popliteal block spares them, a subgluteal block does not.
The higher you block, the more you catch; the lower you block, the shallower and safer it is.

A purely sensory nerve from S1–S3. It is a branch of the sacral plexus, not of the sciatic nerve: it leaves the pelvis with the sciatic nerve below piriformis and runs down under gluteus maximus superficial to it, beside the inferior gluteal vessels. High in the buttock it lies medial to the sciatic nerve; at the gluteal crease its side varies and on ultrasound it is often slightly lateral. Subgluteal sciatic block

The sciatic nerve at the gluteal crease, in the plane under gluteus maximus between the ischial tuberosity and the femur. It numbs everything below the knee except the saphenous strip, plus the hamstrings and the back of the knee joint, so it works above a mid-thigh cut (with femoral, obturator and lateral femoral cutaneous blocks). Its blind spot is the skin of the back of the thigh: the posterior femoral cutaneous nerve lies beside it behind a fascia and is often missed.

Below-knee amputation with a thigh cuff

100 mm echogenic (150 mm if obese), in-plane, lateral to medial

Below the knee except the saphenous strip; the hamstrings; the back of the knee joint (not its skin). Not reliably the back of the thigh.

Position

Lateral (Sims), block side up, the upper hip and knee flexed so the gluteal crease opens; the lower leg straight. Prone is easiest for scanning if the patient can manage it. Expose the foot to see the twitch. For a patient who cannot turn (fracture, sick, external fixator), use the anterior approach supine, or lift the leg (hip and knee flexed, held by an assistant) for a supine subgluteal approach.

Equipment
Low-frequency curvilinear probe (a linear probe may do in a slim patient)

Nerve stimulator (dual guidance helps at this depth): set about 0.5 mA

Landmarks and scanning

Feel the ischial tuberosity and the greater trochanter. The nerve runs down roughly midway between them, a little nearer the ischium. Put the probe transverse on the gluteal crease between the two.

Two bones, one oval: find the ischium (medial) and the femur (lateral) as bright lines with shadows; the nerve lies between them, under the bright fascia of gluteus maximus.
Can’t see it? Tilt the probe (the nerve is very anisotropic); ask the patient to move the foot (the nerve rocks); or start in the popliteal fossa, where it is easy, and trace it up.
Depth: several centimetres, more in the obese and deeper again at the transgluteal level. Start with the depth set deep, then set the focus at the nerve.
Colour Doppler: a small artery runs on the nerve (from the inferior gluteal artery).
Needle approach

In-plane, lateral to medial, entering 1–2 cm lateral to the probe. The path is steep: angle the probe slightly (heel-toe) to see the needle better. Feel the give through the fascia under gluteus maximus. Aim for the lateral corner of the nerve. Out-of-plane from caudal works too and suits a catheter.

MECHANISM

At the gluteal crease the sciatic nerve is still one trunk: the tibial division (medial) and the common peroneal division (lateral) in one sheath. It has no skin branches in the thigh, but it still carries the branches to the hamstrings (from its medial side, in the upper thigh), the posterior knee joint branches and everything below the knee. The posterior femoral cutaneous nerve runs beside it under gluteus maximus but is separated from it by a fascia at this level, so fluid around the sciatic nerve often does not reach it.

HOW DENSE, HOW RELIABLE

Dense surgical anaesthesia below the knee and complete motor block (no knee flexion, no ankle or toe movement) when the nerve is surrounded. Onset is slower than at the popliteal fossa: test at 20–30 minutes, in the tibial (sole), common peroneal (dorsum, first web space) and sural (lateral foot) territories, and the back of the thigh if the posterior femoral cutaneous nerve matters.

WHAT IT MISSES
The saphenous strip (medial leg and ankle): add a saphenous or adductor canal block, or a femoral block.
The front, lateral and medial thigh (femoral, lateral femoral cutaneous, obturator).
The back of the thigh in many patients: add a posterior femoral cutaneous injection, or use a transgluteal or parasacral approach.
The hip joint (it is below the hip branches).
Complications and how to avoid them
Falls and weakness: no knee flexion and a foot drop. The patient cannot stand on the leg; warn them, protect the heel, use a splint or boot as needed.
Nerve injury: the sciatic nerve is big, deep and hard to see well; intraneural injection was seen on video in about one in six subgluteal blocks in one series (without lasting harm, but no comfort). Low current, low pressure, no paraesthesia, stop if the nerve swells. The common peroneal division is the more vulnerable.
Masked injury or compartment syndrome: after hip surgery (sciatic nerve at risk from retractors and dislocation) and in leg trauma, agree with the surgeon before blocking, or block after the neurological check.
Vascular puncture: inferior gluteal vessels at the higher levels; femoral and profunda vessels on the anterior approach. Deep and non-compressible at the transgluteal, parasacral and anterior sites: matters in the anticoagulated.
Local anaesthetic toxicity when it is one of four or five blocks: count the milligrams.
Pressure injury of the numb heel and the back of the leg; long-lasting block after high concentrations.
Practical pearls
Two bones, one oval: ischium medial, femur lateral, nerve in between under gluteus maximus.
Lost the nerve? Trace it up from the popliteal fossa.
Anisotropic: tilt the probe until the oval lights up.
Under it first, then over it: the nerve should float, not swell.
Twitch the foot, not the buttock or the hamstrings.
Subgluteal: the posterior femoral cutaneous nerve lies beside the sciatic nerve but behind a fascia, so the back of the thigh may stay sensate.
Higher (transgluteal, parasacral) catches the back of the thigh; lower (popliteal) spares the hamstrings.
Supine and can’t turn? Anterior approach, 6–8 cm deep, medial to the femoral vessels.
A big nerve is slow: allow 20–30 minutes before you test.
Sciatic block for a knee replacement masks a peroneal palsy: discuss first.
Four levels compared: parasacral, transgluteal, subgluteal, anterior

The higher you block, the more neighbouring sacral plexus branches you catch. The posterior femoral cutaneous and inferior gluteal nerves leave the pelvis with the sciatic nerve (the superior gluteal nerve above piriformis) and part company with it in the buttock; none of them is a branch of the sciatic nerve. The lower you block, the easier and shallower it is, and the more you spare. The levels figure in the anatomy chapter shows the same thing on a drawing.

Transgluteal: sciatic, and often the posterior femoral cutaneous; best for an above-knee amputation.
Subgluteal: sciatic and hamstrings; the back of the thigh not reliably.
Anterior: supine; sciatic only, the back of the thigh stays sensate.

Infragluteal: a few centimetres lower again, where the long head of biceps femoris crosses the nerve; often shallow enough for a linear probe. Same blind spot for the back of the thigh.
Landmark (classic posterior, Labat): lateral, upper leg flexed; a line from the posterior superior iliac spine to the greater trochanter, a perpendicular from its midpoint, and the needle where that meets the line from the greater trochanter to the sacral hiatus. Nerve stimulator to a foot twitch at low current. Know it for the exam; use ultrasound in practice.
Landmark anterior: supine; the needle enters where a perpendicular from the junction of the medial and middle thirds of the inguinal ligament line meets a parallel line through the greater trochanter, and is walked medially off the femur to the nerve. Deep, and the femoral vessels are close.
The posterior femoral cutaneous nerve block

The posterior femoral cutaneous nerve (S1–S3) leaves the pelvis below piriformis with the sciatic nerve and the inferior gluteal vessels, runs down under gluteus maximus superficial to the sciatic nerve (medial to it higher in the buttock; at the gluteal crease its side varies and it is often slightly lateral), and then under the fascia lata down the middle of the back of the thigh. It supplies the skin of the back of the thigh and the popliteal fossa, often the upper calf, the lower buttock (inferior cluneal branches) and part of the perineum. It is purely sensory.

When it matters: above-knee and through-knee amputation (the posterior flap), incisions or skin graft donor sites on the back of the thigh, and a calf or popliteal fossa incision. It matters less for a thigh tourniquet than for an incision: the deep nerves matter most under a cuff, but the skin of the back of the thigh under it is still this nerve.

Ultrasound, subgluteal: from the sciatic view, look just superficial to the sciatic nerve, under gluteus maximus, for a small oval beside a small artery; search the whole superficial surface, as its side varies. A thin fascia separates the two nerves and usually stops fluid crossing between them, so give it its own injection: 5–10 ml of 0.5% ropivacaine (25–50 mg), counted in the total.
Higher up, one needle: at the transgluteal and parasacral levels it lies closer to the sciatic nerve, so the main injection often catches it.
Landmark, at the gluteal crease: a subcutaneous wheal along the crease, plus a few millilitres deep to the fascia at its midpoint (fanned), to catch the nerve before it pierces the fascia. In the mid-thigh, a subcutaneous line about 5 cm above and parallel to the popliteal crease catches its lower branches (with a popliteal block, for varicose vein surgery behind the knee).
Nerve stimulator: which twitch counts
Accept: a twitch of the calf or foot (plantar flexion, inversion, dorsiflexion or eversion) at about 0.3–0.5 mA. Inversion (tibial and deep peroneal together) suggests the tip is near the centre of the nerve and predicts the most complete block; eversion alone suggests you are on the peroneal side.
Don’t accept: a gluteus maximus twitch (you are still in the muscle, or on the inferior gluteal nerve) or a hamstring twitch alone (direct muscle stimulation, or a branch that has already left the trunk).
With ultrasound, use the stimulator as a safety monitor: a twitch at very low current (below about 0.2 mA) suggests the tip is touching or inside the nerve. No twitch does not prove you are outside it.
Catheters
How to place one, and the surgeon’s catheter

A subgluteal catheter gives days of analgesia for an amputation stump or a major foot and ankle reconstruction. Out-of-plane from caudal (the catheter then follows the nerve down), or in-plane from lateral; hydrodissect under the nerve with 5 ml, thread 3–5 cm past the tip, and inject through it while scanning. Tunnel and fix it well: the buttock is a hard place to keep a catheter.

In amputations the surgeon can place a catheter into the sciatic nerve sheath under direct vision before dividing the nerve: simple, reliable, no extra needle. The evidence for both is in the amputation chapter. Run dilute solutions (for example 0.2% ropivacaine); the leg is already weak or gone, so motor block matters less than toxicity.

Consultant corner
Seven subspecialty points
Two nerves in one sheath. The tibial and common peroneal divisions share a sheath down to the popliteal fossa in most people, but in about one in ten they are separate from the pelvis (the common peroneal division may even pass through or above piriformis). If you see two nerves high up, block both.
The obese patient. Injecting into the subgluteal space (the plane under gluteus maximus, on quadratus femoris) rather than chasing the nerve was about twice as fast in overweight patients, with the same success. Fascial-plane thinking works here.
The anticoagulated or septic patient. The transgluteal, parasacral and anterior sites are deep and non-compressible; the subgluteal is intermediate, the popliteal superficial. Use the lowest level that does the job, ultrasound and colour Doppler, a fine needle, and follow your anticoagulation guidance for deep blocks.
The hip. The back of the hip capsule is supplied by the nerve to quadratus femoris, sciatic branches and the superior gluteal nerve, which a parasacral block reaches and a subgluteal block does not. Parasacral plus a lumbar plexus block was the classic complete hip block; today PENG and fascia iliaca cover the front (see the hip page).
Knee surgery. A sciatic block for knee replacement gives good posterior analgesia but a foot drop that masks surgical peroneal nerve injury; PROSPECT does not recommend it. iPACK and a selective tibial block are the motor-sparing answers.
Dual guidance at depth. When the needle is hard to see (steep, deep, obese), the stimulator tells you which side of the nerve you are on, and injection pressure monitoring adds protection.
Fascial plane or perineural? At the subgluteal level both work; perineural (circumferential) spread gives faster, more complete block, the plane approach is quicker and arguably safer. Choose by the image and the patient.
Frontier: what’s new
Five things that are new or being tested
Naming. The 2024 ASRA–ESRA consensus names limb blocks by the nerve and the level: “sciatic nerve block, subgluteal” rather than a list of eponyms, so that trials and records compare like with like.
Percutaneous peripheral nerve stimulation. Fine leads placed near the sciatic and femoral nerves and stimulated for 60 days reduced chronic post-amputation pain in a small placebo-controlled trial, and the benefit lasted to 12 months in most of those treated. The leads do not numb or weaken, which makes them attractive for the stump.
Cryoneurolysis of the sciatic and femoral nerves did not reduce established phantom limb pain in a multicentre sham-controlled trial, and a 2026 pilot that froze all four thigh nerves in people with an above-knee amputation found no benefit either; the large sciatic nerve may simply be too big to freeze through.
Surgery for the nerve itself. Targeted muscle reinnervation joins the cut nerve ends to motor branches of nearby muscles. In a small randomised trial in amputees with established neuroma or phantom pain, it was favoured over excising the neuroma and burying the nerve in muscle; it is increasingly done at the primary amputation. Ask your surgeons whether they do it: it changes where the catheter can go.
Perineural catheters at home. A six-day ambulatory perineural infusion of ropivacaine (sciatic and femoral, or brachial plexus) reduced established phantom limb pain a month later in a multicentre placebo-controlled trial, with little benefit left at a year (see the amputation chapter).
Exam corner

PRACTICE QUESTION

Outline the anatomy of the sciatic nerve from the pelvis to the knee, as relevant to blocking it.

Model answer points
Roots L4–S3, from the sacral plexus; the largest nerve in the body; two divisions in one sheath: tibial (medial, L4–S3) and common peroneal (lateral, L4–S2).
Leaves the pelvis through the greater sciatic foramen below piriformis, with the posterior femoral cutaneous nerve, the inferior gluteal nerve and vessels, and the pudendal nerve (medially).
In the buttock: deep to gluteus maximus, on the posterior surface of the ischium, then on the gemelli, obturator internus and quadratus femoris, about midway between the ischial tuberosity and the greater trochanter.
In the thigh: on adductor magnus, crossed superficially by the long head of biceps femoris; branches to the hamstrings and the hamstring part of adductor magnus (short head of biceps from the peroneal division).
Divides near the apex of the popliteal fossa (level varies; high division in about one in ten).
No cutaneous branches in the thigh: the back of the thigh is the posterior femoral cutaneous nerve. Below the knee: everything except the saphenous territory.

PRACTICE QUESTION

Demonstrate the sciatic nerve at the subgluteal level on this volunteer. What is the subgluteal space? What will a block here not cover?

Model answer points
Lateral (or prone), hips and knees flexed; curvilinear probe transverse at the gluteal crease between the ischial tuberosity and the greater trochanter.
Identify gluteus maximus, its deep fascia, the ischial tuberosity (medial) and femur (lateral) with their shadows, quadratus femoris or adductor magnus deep, and the sciatic nerve: a flat hyperechoic oval or triangle between them.
Subgluteal space: the fascial plane between gluteus maximus (superficial) and quadratus femoris (deep), bounded by the ischial tuberosity and greater trochanter; the sciatic nerve runs in it.
Tricks: tilt for anisotropy; foot movement; trace up from the popliteal fossa.
Not covered: saphenous territory, anterior, lateral and medial thigh (femoral, LFCN, obturator), the hip joint, and often the back of the thigh (posterior femoral cutaneous nerve).

PRACTICE QUESTION

You have done femoral, obturator, lateral femoral cutaneous and subgluteal sciatic blocks for an above-knee amputation. The surgeon’s posterior skin incision hurts. Why, and what will you do?

Model answer points
The posterior thigh skin is the posterior femoral cutaneous nerve, which often escapes a subgluteal sciatic injection (separated by a fascia).
Options: an ultrasound-guided posterior femoral cutaneous injection superficial to the sciatic nerve (if the patient can be positioned), local infiltration by the surgeon along the posterior flap, or sedation and analgesia.
Count the dose already given before adding any more local anaesthetic.
Next time: block it deliberately, or choose a transgluteal level, which more often catches both.

PRACTICE QUESTION

During a nerve stimulator-guided sciatic block in the buttock you see a strong twitch of the buttock at 1 mA. Then a hamstring twitch. Interpret these, and give the endpoint you want.

Model answer points
Buttock twitch: direct gluteus maximus stimulation or the inferior gluteal nerve: too superficial, advance.
Hamstring twitch alone: direct muscle or a hamstring branch: unreliable, redirect.
Wanted: calf or foot twitch (inversion best, then plantar flexion; eversion or dorsiflexion means the peroneal side) at about 0.3–0.5 mA, lost below about 0.2 mA.
With ultrasound: the image and the spread are the endpoint; the stimulator is a safety monitor.

PRACTICE QUESTION

Describe the landmarks for the classic posterior (Labat) and the anterior sciatic nerve blocks. Why has ultrasound largely replaced them?

Model answer points
Classic posterior (Labat): lateral (Sims) position, upper hip and knee flexed. A line from the posterior superior iliac spine to the greater trochanter; a perpendicular from its midpoint, caudally; the needle enters where it meets the line from the greater trochanter to the sacral hiatus. Needle perpendicular to the skin; nerve stimulator to a calf or foot twitch.
Anterior: supine. The inguinal ligament line from the anterior superior iliac spine to the pubic tubercle is trisected; a perpendicular from the junction of its medial and middle thirds meets a parallel line through the greater trochanter. The needle passes posteriorly, is walked medially off the femur (lesser trochanter) and advanced to a foot twitch.
Both are deep, blind and rely on surface landmarks that shift with obesity and position; the anterior path passes close to the femoral vessels.
Ultrasound shows the nerve, the vessels and the spread; it allows a lower volume, fewer passes and a fascial-plane injection (the subgluteal space) when the nerve is hard to see. The landmark methods remain useful as a backup and in exams.

PRACTICE QUESTION

What would you tell a patient when consenting for a subgluteal sciatic block for foot surgery? What are the specific risks?

Model answer points
Expect a numb, heavy leg below the knee with a foot drop and no knee flexion for many hours (often into the next day with long-acting drugs).
Falls: do not walk on the leg until it has recovered; crutches or a splint or boot as advised; protect the numb heel and the back of the leg from pressure.
Nerve injury: transient tingling or numbness is fairly common; lasting injury is rare. Report weakness or numbness that has not recovered when expected.
Masking: the block can hide a surgical peroneal nerve injury or a compartment syndrome; agree with the surgeon beforehand when either is a risk (tibial fractures, knee surgery).
Also: block failure (backup plan), bleeding or bruising (deep site), local anaesthetic toxicity (rare), infection.

Amputation planner: above and below the knee under nerve blocks

The patient is often the sickest on the list: septic, on dual antiplatelets or anticoagulants, with a poor heart. Nerve blocks keep the blood pressure where it is and avoid the airway and the spine. The price is more needles, more milligrams and a plan for every nerve.

RAPID FIRE

Below the knee: two nerves. Popliteal sciatic + saphenous (adductor canal) or femoral.
Above the knee: five nerves. Sciatic, posterior femoral cutaneous, femoral, lateral femoral cutaneous, obturator.
Skip the obturator and the LFCN and the patient will need much more sedation: the medial and lateral thigh will hurt.
Count the milligrams before the first needle. Trim the strength, not the nerves.
A thigh tourniquet under blocks alone is a big ask: avoid it if you can.
Ask the surgeon to place a catheter in the sciatic nerve sheath before dividing it.
Who, and why blocks
The patient: diabetic, vasculopathic, often septic from wet gangrene; ischaemic heart disease and heart failure; renal impairment; on antiplatelets or anticoagulants after failed revascularisation; high opioid use for ischaemic rest pain. Surgery is source control: it rarely waits.
Spinal is excellent when allowed, but sepsis, dual antiplatelets or anticoagulation often rule it out. General anaesthesia in a septic patient with a poor heart risks haemodynamic collapse.
Peripheral nerve blocks keep the circulation stable, are compatible with most anticoagulation at superficial sites, and give hours of analgesia afterwards. In a Singapore series of ASA IV patients having above-knee amputation under blocks, about nine in ten needed no conversion to general or spinal anaesthesia; nearly all had some sedation, and those given only femoral and sciatic blocks needed more of it than those who also had the obturator (and LFCN) blocked.
Arterial line if septic or haemodynamically unstable; group and save or crossmatch, as blood loss depends on the level and on whether a tourniquet is used.

Close to the ceiling. Leave nothing for surgical infiltration; consider a lower strength.

Five nerves cross a mid-thigh cut. The suggested set trims the doses so that four blocks fit under the ceiling for most adults: transgluteal sciatic (which often catches the posterior femoral cutaneous nerve) at 15 ml of 0.5% (a smaller volume keeps the block dense), femoral (15 ml of 0.4%) and LFCN (5 ml of 0.2%) at their standard doses, and obturator at 0.375% (slower and less dense than 0.5%). A teaching set: agree your own with a consultant. Plan sedation as well: almost every patient in published series had some.

Sciatic, transgluteal: Often catches the posterior femoral cutaneous nerve as well (more often than subgluteal).
Choose an operation: the suggested set loads; then switch blocks on and off and change the doses. The leg shows what is numb (solid = dense, dotted = patchy) and where the surgeon cuts. The ceiling used here is 3 mg/kg of ropivacaine, a commonly used figure: use lean weight, and aim lower in the frail, in heart failure and in liver disease. Toxicity from several blocks adds up. A teaching tool, not a prescription.
Doing it: an above-knee amputation under blocks
Plan the dose first. Weigh the patient (lean weight), choose the set, write down the milligrams for each block. Have lipid emulsion in the room.
Sciatic first if the patient can be turned: it is the slowest. Transgluteal (more often catches the posterior femoral cutaneous nerve) or subgluteal plus its own posterior femoral cutaneous injection. Can’t turn? The anterior approach supine, or lift the leg (hip and knee flexed) for a subgluteal view from below.
Then supine, one position: femoral, lateral femoral cutaneous, obturator (proximal, or both divisions distally). A supra-inguinal fascia iliaca covers femoral and LFCN together but does not reliably reach the obturator.
Test each territory at 20–30 minutes: front, outer, inner and back of the thigh at the level of the cut; foot movement for the sciatic.
Sedation plan: titrated, airway-safe, with oxygen and capnography. Ketamine in small doses suits the opioid-tolerant. The surgeon can infiltrate a patchy area, within the dose.
Before the sciatic nerve is divided, ask for a perineural catheter in its sheath (or place your own) for the days after.

WARNING

Gaps that will show

Back of the thigh (posterior flap): posterior femoral cutaneous nerve missed by a subgluteal or anterior sciatic block.
Inner thigh and adductors: obturator. Femoral and fascia iliaca blocks do not reliably reach it.
Outer thigh: lateral femoral cutaneous.
The femur: supplied by all three big nerves; sawing hurts unless femoral, sciatic and obturator are all blocked.
Below-knee amputation
Popliteal sciatic + saphenous covers the skin, muscles, tibia and fibula below the knee. The saphenous block can be at the adductor canal; a femoral block does the same and also numbs the anterior thigh.
Block the popliteal sciatic nerve at or above the division so the lateral sural cutaneous branch (outer upper calf, the lateral end of the incision) is included.
A long posterior flap can reach the territory of the posterior femoral cutaneous nerve high on the calf in some people: if the top of the flap is sensate, the surgeon infiltrates or you add a posterior femoral cutaneous injection.
Anticoagulated patient: the popliteal fossa and adductor canal are superficial and compressible, which is why this is often the anaesthetic of choice when spinal is not allowed.
Guillotine (staged) amputation for sepsis, then a formal amputation days later: a catheter placed at the first operation can serve both.
Tourniquets

Vascular surgeons often amputate without a tourniquet; orthopaedic and trauma surgeons often use one. Tourniquet pain is a deep, ischaemic pain that builds with time; it needs all the nerves of the limb blocked above the cuff (sciatic, femoral, obturator, and the skin under the cuff) and even then is tolerated only for a limited period. For a below-knee amputation under a popliteal block, a calf or no tourniquet fits the block; a thigh cuff does not. The tourniquet guide on the foot and ankle page has more.

Catheters and phantom limb pain

Three kinds of pain follow an amputation: wound (residual limb) pain, which settles with healing; phantom sensations, which nearly everyone has; and phantom limb pain, pain felt in the missing part. About six in ten amputees report phantom pain at some point. Risk factors: severe pain before the amputation, a more proximal (above-knee) amputation, persistent stump pain, a lower-limb amputation and early phantom sensations. Mechanisms run from the cut nerve (neuroma, ectopic firing) through spinal sensitisation to cortical reorganisation.

Perineural catheters (most often placed by the surgeon in the sciatic or tibial nerve sheath, infusing for several days): pooled studies show lower pain scores after surgery; the opioid-sparing effect disappears when only randomised trials are counted; there is no demonstrated effect on phantom pain, chronic stump pain or mortality. Low risk, cheap, and patients are comfortable: worth doing, but don’t promise to prevent phantom pain.
A double-blind trial of perineural levobupivacaine 0.125% (a 10 ml bolus, then 8 ml an hour for four days) after above- and below-knee amputation found no difference in phantom pain at six months, but was underpowered; high early morphine use went with worse phantom pain later. A large UK multicentre trial of surgeon-placed catheters (several hundred patients) has been recruiting; results are awaited.
Pre-emptive epidural analgesia started the day before and continued after amputation did not prevent phantom or stump pain in a randomised trial.
Treating established phantom pain: a six-day ambulatory perineural infusion of ropivacaine (sciatic and femoral, or brachial plexus) reduced established phantom pain a month later in a multicentre placebo-controlled trial, with little benefit left at a year.
For the ward: regular paracetamol, an NSAID only if the kidneys allow, opioid by need (not by habit), and early pain team input. Gabapentinoids have not been shown to prevent phantom pain. Address pain before the operation: it is the strongest risk factor you can still change.
How a surgeon-placed sciatic catheter is usually set up

Before the sciatic nerve is divided, the surgeon passes a catheter (an epidural catheter works) into the nerve sheath, proximally for several centimetres, and brings it out through the skin away from the wound. A bolus (for example 10 ml of 0.125–0.25% bupivacaine-family local anaesthetic) is given before the end of the operation, then an infusion of a few millilitres an hour of a dilute solution for three to five days. Count it in the daily dose, label it clearly as a perineural line, and agree who removes it.

Consultant corner
Five subspecialty points
Mix to save milligrams? Many series used a long-acting drug mixed with lidocaine or mepivacaine for a faster onset and less long-acting drug. The toxicities add: count each drug as a fraction of its own maximum and keep the sum below one. Mixing shortens the block.
Lumbar plexus instead of three blocks? A lumbar plexus (psoas compartment) block covers the femoral and LFCN, and usually the obturator, in one injection, and with a parasacral or transgluteal sciatic it is the textbook anaesthetic for an above-knee amputation. It is deep, close to the epidural space and the kidney, and non-compressible: a poor choice in the anticoagulated, which is most of these patients.
Bilateral amputations: block and operate on one side at a time, and do the second side’s blocks only when the dose allows; or use a different anaesthetic for the second side.
Oedema and infection make the image poor and spread unpredictable: use the stimulator as well, scan away from infected tissue, and prefer levels above the infection.
Delirium, mortality and goals of care: thirty-day mortality after major amputation is high (in the Singapore series, about one in eight at 30 days and nearly half at a year). Blocks avoid opioid-heavy recovery, which helps with delirium; agree ceilings of care before the day.
Frontier: what’s new
Four things that are new or being tested
Targeted muscle reinnervation: surgeons join the cut nerve end to a motor branch of a nearby muscle instead of letting it form a neuroma. In a small randomised trial in amputees with established neuroma or phantom pain, it was favoured over excising and burying the nerve; it is increasingly done at the primary amputation. Regenerative peripheral nerve interfaces (the nerve end wrapped in a small free muscle graft) are an alternative nerve-end operation; they were not part of that trial.
Percutaneous peripheral nerve stimulation of the sciatic and femoral nerves for 60 days reduced chronic post-amputation pain in a small placebo-controlled trial, with benefit at 12 months in most of those treated.
Cryoneurolysis of the sciatic and femoral nerves did not reduce established phantom pain in a multicentre sham-controlled trial; a 2026 pilot freezing all four thigh nerves in above-knee amputees also found no benefit.
Ambulatory catheters: the six-day infusion trial suggests a window to treat established phantom pain at home; whether an early, longer perineural infusion can prevent it is the question the current catheter trials are answering.
Exam corner

MMED OSCE 2020

Which nerves need to be blocked for an above-knee amputation?

Model answer points
Sciatic nerve (above the cut: subgluteal, transgluteal, parasacral or anterior), for the hamstrings, the back of the femur and everything below.
Posterior femoral cutaneous nerve, for the skin of the back of the thigh (posterior flap): caught at the transgluteal or parasacral level, or blocked separately.
Femoral nerve, for the front of the thigh, quadriceps and much of the femur.
Lateral femoral cutaneous nerve, for the outer thigh.
Obturator nerve, for the adductors, part of the femur and a variable patch of inner thigh skin.

PRACTICE QUESTION

A 74-year-old with wet gangrene of the foot, on aspirin and clopidogrel, with an ejection fraction of 25%, is listed for a below-knee amputation tonight. Outline your anaesthetic plan.

Model answer points
Assess: sepsis severity, fluid status, heart failure, renal function, glucose, potassium, coagulation and the antiplatelet timing; goals of care.
Neuraxial is generally avoided on dual antiplatelet therapy; general anaesthesia risks haemodynamic instability.
Plan: ultrasound-guided popliteal sciatic + saphenous (adductor canal) or femoral block, superficial and compressible, with light sedation; arterial line if septic.
Dose: count the total (for example popliteal 15 ml 0.4% + adductor canal 10 ml 0.4% ropivacaine = 100 mg); lipid emulsion available.
No thigh tourniquet (or a calf one); ask the surgeon for a sciatic sheath catheter.
Postoperative: HDU if needed, multimodal analgesia, pain team, delirium prevention; discuss phantom pain.

PRACTICE QUESTION

What is phantom limb pain? How common is it, who gets it, and does a perineural catheter prevent it?

Model answer points
Pain felt in the amputated part, distinct from residual limb (stump) pain and from non-painful phantom sensations.
About six in ten amputees report it at some point.
Risk factors: severe pre-amputation pain, proximal (above-knee) level, persistent stump pain, lower-limb amputation, early phantom sensations.
Mechanisms: peripheral (neuroma, ectopic firing), spinal (central sensitisation), supraspinal (cortical reorganisation).
Perineural catheters lower early pain scores; no proven effect on phantom pain or chronic stump pain. Pre-emptive epidural did not prevent it in a randomised trial.
Treatment of established pain: multimodal and neuropathic agents, mirror therapy and rehabilitation; a six-day perineural infusion reduced established phantom pain at four weeks in one trial; targeted muscle reinnervation for neuroma-related pain.

CHAPTER 4 OF 4 · THIGH AND AMPUTATION BLOCKS

Block combinations for the whole lower limb

One table for the whole leg: the operation, the blocks that cover it, and what they add up to. Each block links to its chapter. Doses are this section’s standard doses; in the big sets a few are trimmed (15 ml for the sciatic, 0.375% for the obturator) so that the set fits the ceiling.

RAPID FIRE

Every block’s milligrams add up, and so does the surgeon’s infiltration.

Big sets: trim the strength, not the nerves; or stage the blocks (one side, then the other).

Below the knee (lateral calf, SPN, sural, sole, heel): sciatic at any level (popliteal, subgluteal); the foot alone by ankle block.
Cluneal (buttock): not a limb block; the inferior cluneal nerves come from the posterior femoral cutaneous nerve.

STEP 1 OF 4 · SCAN

Patient lateral, block side up, hips and knees flexed (or prone). Curvilinear probe, transverse at the gluteal crease, between the two bony landmarks: the ischial tuberosity medially and the femur laterally. Depth 6–8 cm to start. Lost? Start in the popliteal fossa and trace the nerve up.

STEP 2 OF 4 · IDENTIFY

Gluteus maximus superficial, its deep fascia a bright line. Under it, on quadratus femoris (or adductor magnus just below), lies the sciatic nerve: a broad, flat, bright oval or triangle, much wider than it is deep. Tilt the probe to make it pop out, and ask the patient to move the foot: the nerve shifts. The hamstring tendons arise medially from the ischium.

STEP 3 OF 4 · NEEDLE

In-plane, lateral to medial, from the lateral end of the probe. Through gluteus maximus; the fascia under it tents, then gives. Aim for the lateral corner of the nerve, just under it, on quadratus femoris. A foot twitch at about 0.5 mA confirms you are close; a twitch below about 0.2 mA means the tip may be touching or inside the nerve: back off a millimetre.

STEP 4 OF 4 · INJECT

Aspirate, then 2–3 ml: the fluid should lift the nerve off quadratus femoris. The flat oval floats up and its outline sharpens. Then the rest of the first half, aspirating every 5 ml.

STEP 1 OF 4 · SCAN

Lateral, block side up, hips and knees flexed. Curvilinear probe, transverse on the buttock, on the line from the ischial tuberosity to the greater trochanter. Find both bones (bright lines with black shadows); the nerve lies between them. Depth 7–9 cm.

STEP 2 OF 4 · IDENTIFY

Under the thick gluteus maximus, in the subgluteal space on quadratus femoris: the sciatic nerve, a bright flat oval nearer the ischium. Colour Doppler shows the inferior gluteal artery medial to it; the posterior femoral cutaneous nerve runs with the artery, still close to the sciatic nerve at this level.

STEP 3 OF 4 · NEEDLE

In-plane, lateral to medial, 100–150 mm needle. The tip gives through the fascia under gluteus maximus and stops at the lateral edge of the nerve. A twitch of the calf or foot confirms it; a twitch of gluteus maximus alone means you are still in the muscle.

STEP 4 OF 4 · INJECT

The fluid opens the subgluteal space, lifting gluteus maximus and spreading medially over the posterior femoral cutaneous nerve and the artery, and round the sciatic nerve. 20 ml of 0.5% ropivacaine in 5 ml aliquots. One injection here often blocks both nerves, more often than at the gluteal crease.
